analysis.one_liner: Caps damage awards against hospitals and ER doctors when they treat uninsured patients.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote, expiring when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap the money a hospital, emergency room, or its doctors could be ordered to pay an uninsured patient who is injured during emergency care: no more than $250,000 or twice the actual financial losses for pain and suffering, and no more than $250,000 or three times the losses for punitive damages. It would also let courts make a losing patient — or their lawyer, if the lawyer took the case on contingency — pay the winning side's legal fees, and would require judges to tell juries to weigh the effect of any award on the price of malpractice insurance. The limits would apply only to care given without payment to people who had no health coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospitals, emergency departments, doctors employed or contracted by them, and their malpractice insurers would gain: whenever care is furnished to an uninsured person under the federal emergency-care law (EMTALA), total noneconomic damages would be capped at $250,000 or twice the economic damages (whichever is greater), and punitive damages at $250,000 or three times economic damages. Courts could also shift attorney fees and costs onto losing patients or their lawyers in contested cases. [S2][S3]

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals and emergency departments would face sharply lower worst-case liability when treating uninsured patients, whom they are required to screen and stabilize without payment under the federal emergency-care law.
Doctors and physician groups employed by or under contract with those hospitals would be shielded by the same caps, since the bill defines them as emergency care providers.

The bill would give hospitals and providers a tool against lawsuits they view as abusive: courts could order a losing patient — or the patient's contingent-fee lawyer personally — to pay attorney fees and costs, weighing the validity of the claim and the conduct of the litigation.

Supporters of malpractice limits argue that large unpredictable jury awards drive up malpractice insurance costs and push providers away from high-risk emergency work; this bill ties jury instructions directly to that concern by requiring jurors to consider the effect of awards on insurance price and availability.

analysis.who_pays: Uninsured patients who are injured while receiving emergency care would bear the cost, since their compensation for pain and suffering and any punitive award would be capped, and a losing patient — or their contingent-fee lawyer — could be ordered to pay the hospital's legal fees. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Uninsured emergency patients and malpractice plaintiffs

drawbacks.text: The caps would fall hardest on patients whose injuries are catastrophic but mostly non-financial — children, retirees, and people without earnings — because their noneconomic damages would be the largest part of their claim and would be cut to $250,000 regardless of the injury's severity.

The limits would apply only to uninsured patients, creating a two-tier system in which an insured patient injured the same way in the same emergency room could recover full damages while an uninsured one could not.

The fee-shifting provision could chill legitimate claims: a patient with a genuine injury who loses at trial could owe the hospital's legal fees personally, and their contingent-fee lawyer could be liable too, making lawyers reluctant to take hard cases.

Requiring juries to weigh the effect of damages on malpractice insurance prices inserts an industry cost argument into a proceeding whose purpose is to compensate an injured person, and applies to compensatory as well as punitive awards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real but narrow benefit — lower liability exposure for emergency care that hospitals provide without payment, which supporters said would protect access to emergency rooms. The costs fall on a small and vulnerable group: uninsured patients injured by malpractice, who would have their compensation capped and could face personal liability for legal fees if they lost. Because the caps would apply only to patients least able to absorb an injury's financial and personal toll, and only in the emergency setting, the trade-off weighs against the people the bill would have affected directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 22, 2004 and referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action was taken: the committee never reported the bill, and no House or Senate vote ever occurred.
The bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, with all bills not enacted expiring.
Beyond the sponsor and three cosponsors, no member or committee moved the bill at any point in its three-and-a-half-month lifespan.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients' existing right to full jury-awarded damages is undisturbed, since the caps never became law. Hospitals, emergency physicians, and malpractice insurers gained nothing but lost nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, emergency physicians, and malpractice insurers

for.name: Rep. John Shadegg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote it to cap malpractice damages for care given to uninsured emergency patients.

for.name: Reps. Jeff Flake, Charlie Norwood, and Mac Thornberry

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's five sponsors and cosponsors were all House Republicans, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill caps what hospitals and their emergency staff would owe uninsured patients hurt during emergency care — $250,000 or 2x economic damages for noneconomic losses, $250,000 or 3x for punitive damages — and can shift litigation costs onto losing patients or their lawyers. Because their reduced liability comes directly out of injured patients' compensation, their interest runs against those patients here.

industries.industry: Emergency physicians and contracted physician groups
industries.note: Physicians and physician groups under contract with hospitals would get the same damage caps for uncompensated emergency care, lowering their worst-case exposure for treating the uninsured.
The bill requires juries to be instructed to weigh any award's effect on the price and availability of malpractice insurance, and capping payouts directly lowers insurers' exposure on covered claims.

The fee-shifting provision could make a contingent-fee lawyer personally liable for the winning side's fees when a patient loses, raising the risk of taking these cases and discouraging claims on behalf of injured patients.
